So, like, you probably haven’t met Oliver, right? Or maybe you have and just didn’t realize, because he’s got this sort of background-person vibe, but also—well, okay, he stands out if you look for it. His brother, Charles, is the type you’d notice more, but we’ll get to him in a sec. Right now, let’s just say Oliver’s always got mud on his boots. Even when it isn’t raining. Figure that one out.

The funny thing is, they grew up in the same house, with their father, who wasn’t, uh, really fatherly, if you get what I mean. But he was a duke. Which means, supposedly, he’s all dignified and noble, and whatever else dukes are meant to be. But all people talked about was how he loved his old hunting dogs more than his sons. Maybe it was true? Wouldn’t be the weirdest thing.

Now, Orlando enters the picture. He’s Charles’s friend—or sometimes you’d think rival, since they’re like two goats butting heads over everything. Orlando’s got ideas. Big ones. Sometimes too big for the town they live in. He’d roll up to the edge of the estate, stare out at the foggy fields, then say stuff like, “This land’s all bones, I swear.” Which, what does that even mean? But people listened, because Orlando’s got a voice that makes you wanna hear what he says, even if it’s nonsense. Or is it?

Meanwhile, Sir John—that’s another character who just pops up whenever there’s food or trouble (those two go hand in hand for him). Sir John isn’t actually a knight, but insists on the ‘Sir.’ Nobody really argues, because, you know, why pick a fight with a guy who knows where every secret wine cellar is?

So back to the brothers. One rainy night, Charles is pacing outside, muttering about inheritance. You’d think he’d be excited, but nah, he’s wringing his hands and looking like a ghost. Oliver finds him there, huddled under a dying sycamore. “You out here planning a revolution, or just freezing?” Oliver asks, but Charles shakes his head.

The thing is, Charles never really wanted the lands, or the house, or the headaches that come with it. What he wanted—well, he couldn’t say, but it sure wasn’t what was waiting inside that old stone house. Sometimes I wonder, did any of them really want this life, or were they just sort of handed it like a soggy package and told, “Here’s your future, don’t drop it”? Who decides that, huh?

Then the father, the duke, shuffles past with his cane and two dogs trailing, like a parade of the past. He doesn’t say much anymore. If he did, it’d probably just be about the dogs’ latest adventure in the duck pond. There’s a distance between him and his sons like a whole ocean, and no one’s got a boat.

Honestly, I think Oliver always wanted to leave. He’d watch birds a lot, the kind that fly in crooked flocks, not the pretty ones people put on greeting cards. He’d say, “That’s freedom, right there,” but not loud enough for anyone but himself to hear. Why stick around, then? Is it hope, or just habit?

Anyway, one morning, after the mist burned off and left the fields looking almost beautiful, Orlando bursts in with a wild idea about digging up some old well, convinced there’s something amazing hidden down there. Sir John’s already got his sleeves rolled up, thinking there’ll be a bottle if he helps. It turns into this half-baked adventure, mud everywhere, Charles pretending he doesn’t care, but of course he does—he’s got dirt on his shoes to prove it.

They don’t find treasure, unless you count a rusty horseshoe and a pile of broken crockery treasure. Orlando laughs so hard he falls backwards, and for a second, everyone’s just people, not sons or dukes or anything that heavy. Just four muddy guys, making a mess.

Later, when the sun’s nearly gone and the dogs have given up begging for scraps, Charles sits with Oliver by the kitchen door. The cook forgot to shut it and you can smell bread in the air. For once, there’s nothing left to argue about. Maybe tomorrow, something’ll change, or maybe they’ll just keep walking these same old fields, but together, and that isn’t so bad.

Anyway, that’s the story, or at least, that’s how it feels when you’re there. Does any of this matter in the end? Maybe not. But then, maybe it’s just about being seen, even if it’s only by a brother with mud on his boots.

So, you know how it is out on the water, when you’re the first one to set foot on the sand after a long night tossing in the boat? The air’s heavy with salt, and even though it’s supposed to be spring, somehow the wind finds its way right under your coat. Anyway, there was this guy—old Pericles, they called him, but only when he wasn’t around. He would come down to the shore around dawn, every day, looking all thoughtful like he expected some secret to pop right out of the waves. Honestly, I never knew what he was hoping to find. Maybe a message in a bottle or, I don’t know, a sign from the gods or something.

And then there’s Simonides. That’s me, by the way, though pretty much everyone just calls me 'Simon.' I’d like to say I was the village’s best fisherman, but that’d be a stretch—maybe top three if I’m lucky, and only because old Rhys hasn’t caught anything worth talking about in years. Still, I’ve been out before sunrise since I was a kid, so I suppose I know the ropes. Some days, I’ll tell you, fish’ll jump right into your nets, and some other days you’d swear they’ve all packed up and left the sea.

So this morning, well, I was untangling my line, half-listening for the gulls, when Pericles comes pacing up. You ever seen a man so lost in his head he trips over his own feet? That was him that day. He stops, stares at the water, then sort of sighs and glances at me.

“Simonides,” he says, and he always uses my full name, “you ever think about what’s out there?” He points past the rocks, toward the open blue where the sun is just starting to break up the mist.

Well, what do you say to that? I shrugged, said, “Fish, I hope.” 

He laughs, but it’s a tired sort of laugh, you know? The kind people use when they’ve got bigger worries than fish. “No,” he says, “I mean, really—do you ever feel as though something’s calling you from out there?”

Now, I’d like to say I’m the kind of fellow who’s got answers for everything. But I guess I sort of shifted my feet and mumbled something about the only thing that ever called me was an empty stomach.

Pericles just keeps on staring. “I had a dream of Thaisa,” he says. His voice gets real quiet, and I almost pretend not to hear. “She was standing on the shore, just—just over there, by the old willow. She called to me. And it was her, I know it was.” 

The thing is, most folks don’t talk too much about Thaisa anymore. She was his wife, or maybe more like a legend by now—disappeared in a storm, years back. Some say she drowned, some say she ran off to another village, but you know how stories grow around here. All I know is, Pericles never quite got over it.

So, I didn’t want to poke at old wounds. But I had to say something, right? “You figure dreams mean something, sir?” I asked, trying to keep my voice steady.

He smiled, that sad way he does. “Sometimes. Sometimes I think it’s just the sea, whispering in my sleep. Other times, I think… maybe I’m meant to go after her.”

Now, tell me, what would you do if a man like Pericles turned to you and said he might be pulled out to sea by a voice only he could hear? There’s not much you can do, really. I tried to joke. “Well then, you’ll need a bigger net, sir.”

He actually chuckled, a real one this time, and patted my shoulder. But I could see it in his eyes—he’d already set sail in his head, whether his boat left shore or not.

So, we fished. Caught two mackerel, nothing special. The sun came up, burned off the grey. Pericles wandered off by noon, same as always, and I packed up my catch and started up the path. I always pass that old willow on my way home. Call me superstitious, but sometimes the hairs on my neck stand up there, like someone’s watching. Is it just the wind, or do old stories hang around longer than we think?

Anyway, that’s how it goes. The fish come in, the fish go out. The sea keeps her secrets, and men like Pericles keep listening. And me? I just mend my nets and wait for tomorrow, same as always.

So uh, this is a pretty weird story, but you wanted one, so here goes. There was this guy, his name was—well, I’m not gonna say his name straight out because, you know, names have power or whatever, but let’s call him “R.” So, R was, you know, kind of a mess in the way that people get when they’re young and think they know how it all works, but I don’t think he really did. He’d wander around at night, just talking to himself, or maybe not talking, more like muttering. 

The thing is, he had this huge thing for a girl. And, ugh, can you believe it? Her folks hated his, like, ancient, grudge-style hatred where nobody can even remember why they’re mad. So, anyway, this guy—R—he would hang out under her window and sometimes throw rocks but, you know, carefully, because he didn’t wanna break anything. He’d say stuff like, “If only my name wasn’t mine,” and then get all quiet like he’d said something important. What’s a name, really, you know? Sometimes you start wondering if you’re just all the labels people stick on you or if you can be more than that.

I mean, how much do names matter? Like, if I woke up tomorrow and everyone called me “Zebra,” would I start acting stripy and wild? Or would I just stay myself and get used to being shouted at in a new way? That’s the kind of dumb question “R” would actually ask. And if you called him out—like, “Hey, you’re being dramatic”—he’d just sigh and look at the moon like it owed him money.

But, sorry, back on track. One night, the girl—let’s call her “J”—shows up at her window and she’s got this serious look, like she’s been waiting her whole life to say something. R nearly falls over seeing her, and starts in with, “What’s in a name?” and all that. He thinks if he could just drop his name, everything would be fine. Like, presto, all the problems vanish. But would they? If he was still who he was inside, would anything really change, or would the world just find something else to gripe about?

J shakes her head—she’s got this way of listening, but not letting him get away with stuff. She says, “Would you toss away everything for me?” and R tries to make some big speech, but he can’t get the words out in the right order. Have you ever tried to say something important and just ended up babbling? Happens all the time to me. Words get stuck. It's like the more you care, the harder it gets.

So anyway, the two of them go back and forth, and, honestly, it’s about as awkward as you’d expect. Love can be, what, clumsy? It’s not all perfect lines and swooning. Sometimes it’s just two people tripping over how much they wish things were easier. Like, wouldn’t it be nice if the world just chilled out and let people love who they wanted to, no drama? Ha—good one, right?

But here’s the weird part. R tries to make a promise—he starts with, “By thy name, I swear,” or something, then he stops and laughs. He says, “Wait, what am I even swearing by? The thing I said I’d give up?” and they both just crack up. The moon looks on, and, well, I dunno if the moon cared, but it was there.

You ever notice moments like that sort of float? Like, maybe they don’t solve anything, but for a second, you feel lighter, like the world’s nonsense doesn’t stick quite so hard. The two of them—R and J—they decide, right there, that love isn’t about the name or the old stories or anybody else’s rules. It’s about… well, nobody really knows, do they? Maybe it’s just about trying. 

So, they stand under the window, not knowing what’s next, but kind of okay with it. R says, “I love thee, whatever they call me or you or anything.” J grins and just says, “Good,” and honestly, that’s enough for the night.

That’s it, really. No fancy ending. Just people hoping the world lets them be themselves for once. Do you suppose that ever happens?

So, the thing is, Timon’s house used to be the one with the golden roof — not really gold, of course, but you’d look at it and for a second, you’d buy it. He threw open those double doors every night like he wanted to let in the whole city. Lords, poets, hangers-on, folks looking for a free drink — they all crowded in, laughing too loud, talking too fast. There was a story going round that some guy, a merchant or a painter or, I don’t know, a juggler, once walked in not even knowing Timon, and left with a horse and a bag of coins.

But now? You’d walk up his drive and see weeds taller than your head, windows all dusty, that golden color faded to something that looks like, I don’t know, like rain on pavement. The only person coming and going anymore is Flavius. He’s Timon’s steward — loyal to a fault. You get the sense he’s the last one holding the place together, but for what? Who’s he keeping the house for? Timon barely eats, sits with his back to the fire most nights, muttering to himself. And if you ask where the lords went, or all those bright-eyed friends — well, aren’t you just asking for disappointment?

I saw Apemantus out there once too. He’s something else, that guy. You never know if he’s making fun of you or just stating facts, but he’s always scowling like someone put vinegar in his wine. He stood in Timon’s hall, looked around, and just said, “Well, you’ve emptied your purse, and emptied your house right after. Who’s the fool?” But Timon just shrugged. He didn’t even argue. He mostly doesn’t bother anymore. Is it just me, or do people get tired even of being angry? Maybe there’s only so much cursing one person can manage before it all feels pointless.

Sometimes, when Timon’s not in his own head, he’ll ask Flavius about old friends. “What about Lord Lucius?” he’ll say. “He owed me a favor.” And Flavius, poor soul, he’ll say he sent messages, but nobody answered. Doesn’t that sting? Giving everything you’ve got to folks who vanish at the first sign you might need something back. Do you think people are selfish by nature, or is it just easy to forget the hand that fed you once you’re full?

Timon used to bless everyone who visited — I mean, really, like toast to their good health, wish them luck, all that. Now he looks tired even when he tries to smile. And sometimes he says stuff that doesn’t even make sense, like, “The sun’s nothing but a lamp burning out.” I don’t know what that means, honestly. Maybe it’s how it gets when you’ve seen so much hope slip away.

But Flavius keeps going. He sweeps, he lights candles, he fixes the drapes no one’s looking at. He still calls Timon “my lord”, even when there’s no one left to hear. That kind of loyalty, it’s either heartwarming or just sad. Depends how you see it.

I’ll tell you, one night I stayed late in the kitchen, just passing time with the old cook, and we heard Timon stomping around in the dark, cursing the walls, like the house itself had betrayed him, not the people. The cook just shook his head, said, “When the gold’s gone, so’s the laughter.” That stuck with me.

So, days pass, nights drag on, and the city forgets Timon. He could’ve been remembered as a generous soul, I guess, but who writes down the stories of men who give everything away? One morning, I saw Flavius standing out front, waiting for a letter or a knock that didn’t come, and I thought, well, maybe that’s the real fool’s errand — hoping people remember, or care, or come back.

And honestly, I can’t decide if Timon’s the idiot for loving people so much, or if everyone else is for forgetting him the second the silver ran dry. Maybe that’s just how it goes, though. Not sure. All I know is, the house is quiet now. Too quiet. Sometimes, you almost think you can hear laughter echoing off the empty walls, but it’s just the wind. Or maybe ghosts, who knows.

So, let’s just—well, look, I’ll start from where I remember. It was Martius, yeah, always kind of, I don’t know, he just had that blunt way about him, right? Not exactly the guy you’d take to a festival if you wanted to have fun, but for getting stuff done, you’d want him right there. And so it happened, or maybe it nearly did (memory’s weird), but he and Cominius were standing out by that ugly old wall near the gate, watching soldiers shuffle around. Lartius was supposed to meet them, but, you know, he’s late. Typical.

The thing is, Martius couldn’t sit still at all. He kept clapping mud off his gloves, pacing back and forth, and it’s like—honestly, why do people like him get stuck waiting around so much? He’s built for action. So he starts in, “Cominius, we could be halfway to Aufidius’ camp by now, if folks would just pull together instead of talking everything apart.” And Cominius just shrugs, but you can tell he’s tired of all the noise too.

Maybe you’re wondering what any of this has to do with anything, but, well, I guess it’s the way they all acted that kind of sticks with me. It was like nobody could agree on what was actually ‘good’ for us, or the city, or whatever. Everyone had a different story. Martius thought it was simple—you’re either on the side that fixes what’s wrong, or you’re the thing that’s wrong. Hard lines, no gray zone. But Cominius, and Lartius too when he finally got there, kept trying to talk things through. “Let’s not rush, let’s hear both sides, let’s be careful.” That sort of thing. Does being careful ever make a difference when things are falling apart, though?

And all the while, little rumors about Aufidius are floating around, like dark water under a bridge. That he’s gathering more folks, or he’s got spies—can’t ever pin it down, but it gets people nervous. Martius kind of fed off that, almost got sharper with every new bit of bad news. Sometimes, I thought maybe he actually wanted the fight just to cut through all the noise. There was this weird moment, I remember it pretty clear, where Martius just turns and asks—half to himself, half to us—“If we know what needs doing, what’s the point in waiting for someone else to say so?” And, well, you know, no one said anything for a bit.

Lartius, he’s always the practical one, starts talking about moving supplies, getting the gates checked. You’d think they’d be working together by then, but you could feel something pulling apart underneath, like, I don’t know, a rope fraying where nobody’s looking.

Later that day, after the dust and the yelling, I saw Martius by himself over by the wall. He looked angry, but not the good kind. Not the kind that makes you want to, you know, do something bold. It was heavy and cold. Like he was carrying a rock nobody else could see. People kept saying he’d done good. But good’s a slippery word, isn’t it? What does it even mean, when everyone sees it different? 

Honestly, I’m not sure what happened with Aufidius in the end. The stories got tangled, and there’s always another war or peace or argument coming right after. But—uh—I’ll tell you, sometimes, when you’re out by the wall, you can almost feel old Martius’ footsteps still there. People talk about honor and duty and all that, but they never tell you how it’s supposed to feel after you’ve done what needed doing. Would you want to know?

In any case, I guess some things keep going. Even when people change, or names get lost, there’s always someone standing at a wall, deciding if they should wait or go. And, uh, maybe that’s the real question. If you knew what needed doing, would you just get on with it, or would you wait for someone else to tell you it’s alright?

So, here's the thing: there was this old king and—look, I know what you’re probably thinking, another king story, but just hear me out—he wasn’t just old, he was also, like, tired of everyone’s nonsense. You could see it in the way his eyes drifted off whenever someone tried to flatter him. And, uh, he had this chamberlain, old as him, maybe older, named Mr. Giles or maybe just Giles. I’m not sure anyone called him “mister” to his face, but he had that sort of groaning dignity anyway.

There was a lady called Anne who kinda floated around the edges of the hall, always in dresses that looked like they came from another time. People said she was related to someone important, I dunno, maybe the king’s cousin’s cousin or something. She had a habit of smiling at everyone like she knew some secret. I guess—well, I guess everyone thought she was nice, but maybe not good in the way chamberlain Giles was good. You know how some people just do stuff for the sake of doing good? Yeah, that was Giles, not Anne.

The palace wasn’t fancy, not how you’d imagine. The floors creaked and the tapestries had moth holes. There were mice sometimes. Okay, a lot. The king tried to pretend he didn’t notice, but Anne always looked at the skittering creatures as if she knew they might just be smarter than most of the court.

So one morning, the king woke up cranky—like, crack-of-dawn, can’t-sleep sort of cranky. He shuffled down the main stairs (carefully, because, y’know, he’s old) and said—well, sort of barked—“Where’s my chamberlain?” Giles, who’d been up before the sun, shuffled in and bowed so low it looked like his back might snap. And the king waved at him, kinda dismissive.

I mean, have you ever seen two people who trust each other so much they talk in half sentences? That was them. The king would say “The thing with the accounts—” and Giles would nod and already be heading for the treasury. No wasted words. Anne would watch from the doorway, not getting in the way, just listening. Maybe learning, I dunno.

Here’s where everything started to go weird. The thing is, Anne—see, she wasn’t content to just stand there smiling forever. One day, when the king was distracted by arguing with his cook about whether salt belonged in porridge, she drifted over to Giles and said, “Do you think the king is happy?” What do you even say to that? Giles just raised an eyebrow and said, “It’s not my place to know.”

Anne sorta laughed, soft and kind of sad. She said, “If you were king, what would you do different?” Giles shuffled his feet, looked at his shoes. I guess he’d never thought about that because he just mumbled something about “doing good is more important than being king.” Was that wise or just obvious? Who knows.

Later that night—well, it was more like evening, but it gets dark early in autumn—Anne found the king alone in the garden. He didn’t look surprised, just tired. She asked if he’d ever wanted to run away. He smiled for the first time anyone could remember, which was honestly almost unsettling. “Of course,” he said, “but who’d look after Giles?” That was the closest he got to admitting anything, I think.

So they sat there for a while. The garden wasn’t much, just some overgrown hedges and one very stubborn rosebush. Anne picked at the thorns, and the king watched her, like he was waiting for her to ask him for something. But she never did, not that night. They just listened to the wind, and maybe the mice scrabbling around in the ivy.

The next morning, everything was, I dunno, a little lighter. The king grumbled less. Giles brought out tea for two instead of just for one. Anne smiled the same way, but now it seemed more, real? Something had shifted, like, quietly. And nobody said anything about it. Maybe that’s how things change, little by little, two people at a time. Or maybe it takes more. Is that silly? Maybe. But honestly, what else is there—if not small, good things that nobody notices except two or three people, and probably some mice?

Okay, uh, so let me try to explain what happened that night because—well, honestly, I still can’t quite figure it out myself. You know how sometimes you think you’re doing something smart but, like, the moment you start, everything just goes sideways? That’s kinda what went down with me and Pete. We’d been sitting under that busted streetlight on Fifth, fiddling with our phones, talking about how Raz once said anybody with half a brain would just… I don’t know, take off when things get bad. Maybe he was on to something.

Anyway, we’d been talking and, listen, Pete’s advice never really makes sense, but I let him go on about it. He kept saying, “You’ve gotta let things play out, you can’t just jump in and try to fix everything.” But me, I can’t leave well enough alone. It’s just not in me. Which is, uh, probably why I got involved when I did.

So, right, here’s the thing: there was this guy—he didn’t really look right. Like, not dangerous or anything, just… off. A real Raskolnikov type if you ask me—always looking at the ground, mumbling to himself, carrying a bag that seemed way too heavy for whatever was in it. Pete, of course, wanted to let him be. “Don’t be a fool, man,” he said, but I’d already stood up and started walking over, so whatever.

As I got close, the guy looked up. And, uh, I swear, there was this flash of something in his eyes. Maybe fear? Maybe he just hated that I was there. Either way, it made me pause. Which, looking back, was probably smart, but of course I kept going because, well, I don’t listen to my own instincts, do I? I said, “Hey, you alright?” and he didn’t answer. Not at first, anyway. Then he muttered, almost too quiet for me to hear, “Leave me alone.” You ever have one of those moments where you know you should just do what’s asked and walk away but you just… can’t? Would it have been easier if I’d just listened?

But no, I asked again, and the second time, he finally looked at me. His eyes were wild, but, like, tired too, if that makes sense. “You don’t get it,” he said, and I honestly didn’t. “Don’t you see?” he snapped, and, well, I didn’t see anything except a dude on the edge. I probably looked like a total fool standing there, but I couldn’t help myself. “Tell me, man. I wanna know.”

He sighed so heavy it was almost a groan. “Nothing to tell,” he said. I almost believed him, but then he stood up real sudden and the bag hit the pavement, making a sort of dull clunk. Pete was still back by the light, waving at me to come back, but I just stood there like I couldn’t move. I don’t even know why. Maybe I thought I could help, or maybe I just didn’t want to be alone in my own head that night.

Out of nowhere, the guy started walking away, real fast. I almost followed, honestly, but something stopped me. Like, this is where it all breaks, you know? It’s one of those crossroads you read about, except it doesn’t feel dramatic, it just feels… sad, I guess. I let him go, eventually, and I guess I’ll never know what was really in that bag or what he was running from. Pete called me over, and we stood there for a while not saying much.

Do you ever wonder if you’re supposed to just let people go? Or is it better to run after them, to try to help, even if you don’t have the first clue what you’re supposed to do or say? I wish I knew. But that night, I just watched him vanish into the shadow under the old bridge, and I couldn’t tell if I’d dodged something or just missed my chance to actually do something right for once.

Anyway, that’s what happened. Not much to it, really, but I keep thinking about that guy, and what I could’ve done different. Maybe I am just as much a fool as Pete always says.

So, yeah, I mean—look, it’s late and you probably just want the story, but the thing is: I can’t really remember how it started. It’s fuzzy. Was it raining? Maybe. Or maybe it was sunny and I’m just mixing it up with another afternoon. There’s this pub, right, over by the river where the old bridge used to be, and everyone always talks about the food—like, it’s got the best leeks in soup in town. That’s a weird thing to be famous for, but, hey, people still come in droves.

Okay, I’ll get to the point. Fluellen’s working behind the bar, trying to look busy, but he’s got this vibe, y’know, like he’s the only good guy in the joint. He’s wiping the counter—some sticky stuff, don’t ask me what, and muttering about how no one appreciates a proper leek. “Leek’s a good vegetable,” he says to nobody in particular. I mean, is it? I don’t know. I just eat whatever’s in front of me. But Fluellen’s got beef about it, thinks people should pray for the leek at dinner, not just wolf it down. He’s got this big Welsh pride about it, too, which is cool and all, but, honestly, does anyone even care?

There’s this knave—I swear, that’s the best word for him—lurking at the end of the bar. He’s got a pistol tucked under his coat and, yeah, I saw him flash it when he thought no one was looking. But Fluellen saw it, too, because that guy misses nothing. The knave’s got a face you wanna punch, but you don’t, because he also looks like he’d bite. So, anyway, the knave orders some food, asks Fluellen for the “French stuff,” which, I guess, means fries or something fancier. Fluellen just gives him the look, y’know, like he’s about to drop him through the floor.

I’m sitting there, eating—no, more like picking at my food, because, honestly, I don’t know if it’s worth the effort. The leek’s alright. It’s green. It tastes like...well, like a leek. But I nod anyway when Fluellen asks if it’s good, because why not. I don’t wanna mess with him, not tonight. He’s got that tired energy. You ever see someone who looks like they’re holding the whole world up by themselves? That’s him.

The knave gets twitchy, starts yammering about something in French that I don’t understand, maybe cursing or maybe just asking for a drink. Fluellen ignores him, gets all worked up and starts on about how people should eat more leeks and respect their roots. I mean, really, who cares about leeks? Is anyone actually listening? Well, I’m half-listening, but mostly because I don’t want to miss the moment the pistol comes out. It’s stupid, but you get bored and start expecting drama.

Suddenly, the knave stands up—way too fast, chair scraping—and everyone goes quiet. He’s got that wild look, like he’s about to do something dumb. He shouts, “Pray for your French food, you fools!” and—I mean, what?—he sounds insane. Fluellen doesn’t flinch, just walks over and puts his hand out. I’m thinking, is this the part where someone gets shot? But nope, Fluellen just tugs the knave’s coat until the pistol falls out. It’s not even loaded, turns out. The knave looks even smaller, somehow, once he’s lost the pistol.

“Eat your leek,” Fluellen says, pushing a bowl in front of him. The knave hesitates, glances at me, like I’m gonna help him. I shrug. Eat your leek, man. The world’s rough, but you gotta eat.

So, the knave slumps down and starts eating, mumbling in French—maybe about how leeks aren’t so bad, maybe about wanting to go home. Fluellen’s got this calm thing going now, wiping the bar again, saying, “Good food makes good people.” Nobody knows what that really means, but it sounds nice. I finish my soup, which tastes better suddenly—not sure why. Maybe it’s just relief.

I mean, what makes a pub safe? Is it the food, or is it the people who care enough to stand up even when things get weird? Fluellen’s still working, smiling a bit, and everyone starts talking again, like nothing happened.

So yeah, that’s it, I guess. Leek soup, a knave, a pistol, and a little bit of French.

So, I thought I’d write this out, just to get things straight, because honestly, I haven’t got anyone to talk to who’d really understand, and I’m starting to feel like I might explode if I don’t just, you know, put it somewhere. You ever get that feeling? Like your head’s so full of thoughts you could just scream? Anyway, I guess this is sorta like a letter—though it’s not really for anybody in particular, and, well, I’m not sure if it’d matter if it was.

The thing is, two months ago—yeah, it’s been that long—I started thinking a lot about god, or, I guess, whatever people believe god is. Which is weird for me, because I don’t usually get all, you know, spiritual or philosophical or anything. I mean, I grew up hearing a bunch of stuff about god and church and “doing the right thing,” but I always felt kinda skeptical, like, who decides what that even means? And honestly, nobody’s ever given me a real answer. Still, when you’re alone and time starts dragging, your mind just goes places. Maybe it’s boredom, maybe it’s something else. Who knows?

So, I found myself writing a letter that I never sent—yeah, I do that, write letters to people or things or whatever, just to make sense of my mess. This one was to god, though I didn’t really know what I wanted to say, and I definitely didn’t know what I wanted back. Which brings me to the question: if you could talk to god, what would you ask? Or maybe—what would you want to know?

I wrote about needing clarity, about wanting answers, but mostly about wanting to feel like I mattered. That sounds cheesy, I know, but after one of those days where you drop your keys, lose your phone, spill coffee all over your shirt and get yelled at for something you didn’t do, you kinda start wondering if anybody’s out there listening, or if you’re just talking to yourself.

Months slipped by, and nothing changed, really. Well, except I started paying attention to stuff I used to ignore, like little lessons. You know, things you pick up when you’re forced to sit still—like how the neighbor’s dog barks at exactly 6:07 every single morning, or how the sun hits the kitchen table just right for about fourteen minutes, which, for some reason, made me think of childhood breakfasts and my dad’s terrible jokes. I think there are lessons everywhere, but they’re not spelled out, not written down like “here’s what you need to know”—they’re just, I dunno, floating there, waiting. Is that how life works? Like, you gotta pay attention or you miss everything?

Anyway, the letter stayed in my drawer. I kept adding stuff to it—random questions, half-thoughts, apologies, jokes that would make no sense to anyone but me. I even wrote, “If you’re reading this, I hope you think I’m funny,” which might be the most desperate thing I’ve ever scribbled, but who cares? Maybe god likes jokes.

And then, I realized I wasn’t all that interested in answers. I mean, sure, I wanted them, but wanting and needing are different. Over time, I just wanted connection. Like, the act of writing itself made me feel less alone, even if the only person reading was me. Maybe that’s what everyone’s after—connection, not answers.

Sometimes, when I’m sitting around waiting for the bus, or trying to fall asleep, I wonder if anyone else does this—writes stupid letters to nobody, hopes someone, or something, will care. I have friends, but I don’t talk to them about this stuff. They’d probably laugh or tell me to get over myself. That’s fine, I guess. Everybody’s got their own stuff.

So, I don’t really know what god is now. I thought I’d know after two months, or at least understand something more, but I honestly don’t. Maybe god’s just an idea, or a hope, or maybe god’s the lessons you notice when you finally stop to pay attention. Or, maybe, god’s just the feeling you get when you’re writing letters to nobody and still feel seen, somehow. I know that’s not an answer, but it’s what I got.

All I know is, I’ll keep writing. Maybe next time I’ll send a letter, or maybe I’ll just keep tossing them in drawers, and that’ll be enough. That’s the thing about wanting—you never really stop, but maybe you start wanting different things. Fewer answers, more connection. Less noise, more quiet. And, who knows, maybe that’s what god was trying to teach me all along.

So, I guess I should just start at the point where everything kind of went sideways, though to be honest, with us it always went sideways at some point, didn't it? We were a pretty ragtag bunch of friends, stitched together more by, I dunno, time and some shared history than anything else—like, nobody would pick us out in a crowd and think, "Oh, there go the best of chums," not by a long shot. Still, when Paul came staggering into the old café all flushed and out of breath that one rainy Thursday, even old Jules—who barely looked up from his paper most days—couldn't help but raise his eyebrows and say, in that kind of grumpy french way of his, "Qu'est-ce qui se passe, mon ami?" which just means "What's up?" but it sounds fancier.

Paul, well, he's the sort of man you want to believe—tall, got that honest look about him, though if you'd asked me last year, I'd have said he's always a bit too quick to buy some wild story. Anyway, that day he drops his umbrella, nearly takes out my espresso, and blurts out something about losing his job and, well, not just any job but his grandfather's old print shop, which he tried to keep running for the last, what, five years or so? The thing is, we all knew it was a miracle it lasted that long. We all told him to cut his losses, move on, but that's not the sort of thing Paul could ever do. Loyalty's a kind of curse for the unfortunate, if you ask me.

And honestly, I didn't know what to say. I looked to Jules, then to Greta—who was at that ancient game of pretending not to listen while she eavesdropped on the whole thing. She'd always said the shop was doomed, but she liked Paul, maybe more than she let on, and she surprised us all by reaching over, patting his hand, and saying, "We'll figure something out, won't we?" And maybe that's the moment when—look, does every group of friends have that one crisis when you just decide to dig your heels in and help, even if you know, deep down, you're fighting a losing battle? Or is that just the movies?

But anyway, we became a sort of makeshift committee right there. Jules, who hadn't moved faster than a tortoise since the Mitterrand era, offered up an ancient rolodex with names of "kind people, maybe, who remember your grand-père," though his handwriting was so bad that Paul couldn't read half the names. Greta said she'd bake and organize "some kind of fancy french fête," though she didn't know the first thing about actual baking, and I volunteered to redesign the window display, which, in hindsight, was not exactly the lifeboat you'd want in a storm—I'm more the talking sort, not the doing sort.

Days turned into a kind of strange routine—Paul moping, Jules muttering, Greta covered in flour, me fussing with colored paper and string in the dusty front window. Neighbors started popping in with this awkward blend of pity and forced cheerfulness, and, well, I suppose that's humanity for you: sometimes people don't know how to help so they bring you a basil plant or a six-pack, and maybe that does help, sort of. Sometimes the old men who hung around the square, who remembered Paul's grandfather, would come in and tell stories in a mix of French and, well, a kind of local slang that's half poetry and half nonsense.

Did it work? I wish I could say we saved the shop, pulled off a miracle, but life doesn't always hand you those clean happy endings, you know? In the end, Paul packed up the last of the type cases while we just stood there, all of us suddenly aware of how quiet it was without the old presses clattering. Jules raised his cup—wine, not coffee—and said, "To the unfortunate, and the very kind." Greta cried, of course, but that's all right. We left together, a little closer than before, I think.

And I guess that's what you get, in the end. Not what you hoped for, but each other—if you're lucky.

So, okay, here’s what happened with Lucentio—that guy’s always got something up his sleeve. He burst into the courtyard like he’d just heard the king himself was waiting, and poor Biondello nearly tripped over his own feet, trying to follow. I mean, have you ever seen someone so jumpy and at the same time, like, trying to look cool? That’s Biondello for you. He kept tugging at his cap, glancing left and right like he expected someone to drag him off any second. But really, who would care about a servant in this part of town, right?

So anyway, Lucentio grabs him by the elbow—you know, the way someone does when they want to look all serious—and says, “Biondello, you must do something for me, and you must not mess it up.” And Biondello just nods, nods, nods, even before he knows what’s being asked. Hah, good old Biondello, never says no. Is it loyalty or fear? I honestly can’t tell sometimes.

But here’s the thing: Lucentio’s got his eyes on Baptista’s daughter, Katherina. Or, wait, no, no, it’s the younger one he wants—Bianca. See? Even I get mixed up, because all these fathers with their rules and lists of who can marry whom and how much money’s involved—it’s enough to scramble anyone’s brain. And so Baptista, he’s the father, and he’s so proud of his daughters that he can hardly see straight. Thinks he’s the wisest man in Padua, I bet.

So Lucentio’s got a plan, of course. He always does. He says he’ll pretend to be a tutor to get close to Bianca. Can you imagine trying to act like a teacher when your head’s full of, like, hearts and sighs and probably bad poetry? Biondello’s not sure it’ll work, but he’s not stupid enough to say that out loud. You can see it all over his face, though.

And now I guess—well, Lucentio says, “You must go to Baptista’s house and tell him that I, uh, I mean, your master, am a…what did he say? Oh, a scholar from Pisa, come to teach Latin and Greek. Make it sound grand, Biondello. Don’t stutter.” The thing is, Biondello always stutters when he’s nervous. But off he goes, tying his old coat a bit tighter and muttering to himself.

Me? I hung back, pretending to sweep stones off the path just in case anyone asked what I was doing there. But, honestly, I just wanted to see how it all turned out. Wouldn’t you? It’s not like folks fall in love and plot schemes every day around here, though sometimes it feels like it.

I watched Biondello knock at Baptista’s big wooden door, you know, the one with the lion’s head knocker that looks like it’s about to roar? For a second I thought he’d drop dead from nerves, but he managed to get through the speech, more or less. Baptista listened, arms crossed, long white beard twitching. While this was happening, Baptista’s youngest, Bianca, peeked down from the window—just a tiny bit of her face, but enough. Lucentio, who’d snuck around the corner by then, caught her eye. You know that look when two people see each other and the world basically stops? It was kind of like that, only a lot more awkward because her father was right there and poor Lucentio had chalk dust on his sleeve.

Anyway, the conversation took forever. Baptista kept asking questions, like, “Who sent you?” and “Why should I trust some traveling scholar with my daughter’s education?” and Biondello was starting to sweat. I almost wanted to run up and help, but, yeah right, who’d listen to me? At last, though, Baptista agreed to let Lucentio, “the fine scholar from Pisa,” give lessons.

So, everything’s set, at least for now. But tell me, do you really think love ever goes as planned? And why do people always assume fathers know best, anyway? The sun was already slipping behind the rooftops when Lucentio grinned at Biondello and promised him a gold coin—no idea if he’ll ever get it. But the air smelled hopeful, or maybe just like new trouble about to begin. Either way, I couldn’t help but smile as I picked up my broom and moved on.

So, here's the thing: the whole affair started because Mrs. Bell decided she just couldn't stand the smell of horses in the morning anymore. I mean, who could blame her? Imagine the carriages lined up down the lane, all wheels and grumpy drivers and the fog. There was always mist rolling over from the river, like the world was just waking up slow. Anyway, Mrs. Bell marched right over to Mr. Curtis, the head of carriages, or whatever silly thing his title was, and said, "Sir, I would have you know the gentlemen coming to my house aren't to be tripping over your mud."

Now, Mr. Curtis, he was one of those fellows who’d rather talk about the weather than anything real. He tried to smile and doff his hat, said something about "with all due respect ma'am," but Mrs. Bell wasn’t having any of it. She jabbed her umbrella at the nearest wheel, a wobbly old thing, and said, "I expect better." Then she stalked off in a huff, skirts all swooshy.

Funny thing is, the rest of us just watched from the windows. I saw Hamlet, the coach dog—yes, that’s his name—slink behind the boot and sort of squint at the fuss. Hamlet’s got more sense than half the people here, I swear. You ever wonder what dogs think of us when we get all puffed up over mud and manners? Sometimes I think they know something important and just won’t say.

That morning, Osric came by. He's the new gentleman, just in from the city. He's got too-tight boots and the kind of hair that never stays flat, no matter how much he pats it. Osric strolled up with a cocky little grin—like he knew the punchline to a joke no one else heard—and asked Hamlet, "Would you know where a man might find breakfast?" Hamlet sneezed. Osric took it for an answer and headed for the kitchen.

To be honest, the house runs on faith and tea. Mrs. Bell's faith that things will go right, and gallons of tea poured at all hours, mostly by Miss June, the only person who can carry three saucers without dropping one. Miss June says, "If gentlemen'd stop asking for toast at midnight, I’d sleep more." And she laughs, but you can see she means it. Sometimes I help her, carrying the pots up the back stairs, and she tells me who quarreled and who came home cheerful. Feels like being let in on secrets.

And yet, everyone pretends not to know each other's business. Mr. Curtis acts as if Mrs. Bell's umbrella didn't almost puncture his hat. Osric tips imaginary hats to invisible ladies. Hamlet chases crows off the lawn, which he seems to think is some grand quest. The whole house is a stage. I suppose that's true for every house with guests, though—don't you think?

Yesterday, Sir Tamlin came by. He's an old friend of Mrs. Bell, or something more complicated, but no one ever says. His carriage looked like it'd rolled through a hundred puddles. The driver scowled. Sir Tamlin just waltzed in, all smiles, saying, "Faith, my dear, your drive's cost me a shoe." Mrs. Bell sniffed, "At least you’ve one left." They laughed like old soldiers.

So you get to thinking, why do they all come? It's not the food, which is decent but plain, or the view, which mostly involves fog. Maybe it's the peace, the sense that in this little nest, you can be ridiculous and no one will mind. Even Mrs. Bell. Even Osric. There's a moment after supper, when the fire’s low and everyone talks quietly, not because they're hiding things, but because it feels good to rest.

And things just go on, day to day. Carriages in the morning, arguments about mud, gentlemen who can't find their gloves, Hamlet howling at the moon, Miss June cursing the stairs. Maybe nothing much happens. Still, sometimes when I’m tiptoeing down the hall at night, I wonder if deep down, we all know we’re waiting for something. Or is that just what people do in old houses with too many rooms?

So the thing is, there’s always been something off about Catherine, and—wait, I know that sounds unfair, but hear me out. You know how some people just have that look? Like you walk into a room and you can feel someone’s watching, but you just… you can’t tell who because everyone’s being so normal and drinking whatever bland punch somebody brought, but it’s her. And her eyes, I swear, they’re always a little too bright, catching the light in that way that makes you want to look away but you can’t. I don’t know if I’m explaining this right.

It wasn’t like I was obsessed with her, or whatever—you ever get those weird gut feelings, just for no reason? You can’t shake ’em. I’d see her around, standing off near the window or trailing after the so-called "master," old Mr. Jacobs, who ran the place. Nobody called him that out loud, though. We’d just kind of exchange these glances, you know, the kind where you both know there’s a joke that you’re not saying because it’d be too much effort. Anyway, Catherine would watch him, and sometimes I’d catch her lips moving just a bit, but I couldn’t hear anything, not really.

One afternoon, after most people went out to get lunch, I hung back, pretending to be lost in some crap about supply orders just to avoid the heat outside. Catherine stayed behind too, sitting at one of the desks flipping an old book—looked like the pages were about to fall out. I was about to ask her what she was reading, not really wanting an answer or caring, but instead I just kind of blurted, “Do you ever get tired of this place?” and, wow, why’d I say that? She looked up, real slow, and for a second I thought maybe she’d just ignore me like usual, but she sort of smiled in this way that didn’t really reach her eyes and said, “Sometimes I imagine I’m somewhere else. Somewhere with fewer clocks.”

Isn’t that a weird answer? I mean, what was I supposed to say? There weren’t even that many clocks in the office—three, tops, unless you counted the old grandfather clock that hadn’t worked in years. Sometimes I saw her standing in front of it, though, like she was waiting for it to start ticking again, which is… I don’t know, odd?

Now, here’s the part that sticks with me. A few days later, everyone was buzzing because Mr. Jacobs had lost his glasses and was wandering around half-blind as if the building itself had turned against him. Catherine didn’t say a word, but she had this look that made me think she knew exactly where they were. And later, when I saw her alone in the stairwell, holding those very glasses, she just pressed a finger to her lips like she was telling me to keep quiet, as if it mattered to anyone but him.

I don’t know why, but suddenly I got the urge to ask her if she was happy. I know, it’s none of my business, right? But I did it anyway, kind of mumbling it, half-hoping she wouldn’t hear. But she did. She nodded, slow, and said, “Sometimes, when nobody’s looking, I imagine I’m the one giving orders.”

What does that even mean? I thought about it all day, but I couldn’t get it out of my head. Was she talking about Mr. Jacobs? Or someone else—maybe herself? And honestly, I know I should’ve just left it, but once you start noticing stuff, you can’t un-notice it. Like, I’d catch Catherine in the reflection of the front doors, watching everyone go by, her face all unreadable, and I started wondering if everyone else saw it too, or if it was just me seeing another version of her, one that was waiting for something.

I’m not saying she was dangerous or anything dramatic like that. If anything, she seemed tired, like she was waiting for life to let her in on the big secret. I get that. Who isn’t, sometimes? Still, there’s something that happens when you realize someone’s always in the background, holding on to stuff nobody else knows about—including, apparently, people’s glasses—and yet, they never seem to want the spotlight. Or do they? That’s the thing, right? How can you tell what people really want when you can barely sort out what you want yourself?

So I guess now, every time I run into Catherine, I wonder if she’s still watching, still keeping tabs on everyone, or if she’s finally found a place with fewer clocks and more time for herself. Or maybe, just maybe, she’s the real master after all, and we just haven’t caught on yet

So, uh, let me try and tell you about Timon—yeah, Timon of, well, let's just say from Athens, but it hardly matters where he's from, right? It's not like that stuff sticks with you after you've heard his story. The thing is, Timon started off the kind of friend everyone thinks they want. If you’d met him first, you’d probably think, wow, this guy would give you anything, maybe even his last loaf. And that was true. Almost too true, if I’m being honest.

The thing with Timon is, he didn’t see it coming. Like, not even a hint. His house—it was always open, like, wide open, and if—if you happened to come by hungry or broke or just plain bored, he’d find a way to help. He’d be pulling out coins, food, even little gifts for your kids or whatever. And he laughed easy, like someone who didn’t know there was such a thing as a bad friend.

But you know what happens, right? Or wait, maybe you don’t, but you can probably guess. People talk about Athens being a city where folks look out for each other, but, honestly, if you looked close, it was mostly looking out for themselves. And for a while, Timon didn’t notice. Or maybe he didn’t care. Maybe he thought, like, someday I’ll need a hand and they’ll be there.

Well, the day came. It always does, doesn’t it? I mean, isn’t that the way—first you give, then one day you gotta ask, and that’s when you see what’s what. Anyway, Timon’s luck turned. I couldn’t say how, exactly—maybe he spent too much, maybe thieves, maybe the cost of throwing feast after feast actually bites—doesn’t matter much. Bottom line, he finds himself without, uh, anything. Not even enough for bread. So he knocks on those same doors he kept open so wide, and guess what he gets? Nothing. Not a crumb, not a coin, not even a polite lie.

He tried to laugh it off the first time. “Ah, you must be busy,” he’d say, or, “Next time, then,” and wave and try another friend. The thing is, after a while, you run out of friends to try. Turns out, the word “friend” is easy to use when you’re full and comfortable and the wine hasn’t run out, but it gets real heavy when there’s nothing left to take. Am I making sense? I’m just saying, he realized he was alone in that city, and not just alone, but—what’s worse—forgotten.

So, Timon gets angry. No, not just angry. He turns into someone else entirely. He stops trusting, stops talking, and, uh, I guess you could say he stops living, really. He leaves Athens. Just walks out. Some people said they saw him, dirty and wild, digging up roots to eat. Maybe he’d found gold in the ground once—some folks say that much—but who cares? It’s not about the gold. The whole point is, no one followed him.

And, I mean, can you blame him? If you gave everything away and then when you needed so much as a crust, nobody came, wouldn’t you feel, I don’t know, small and used-up? Do you ever wonder if anyone really means it when they say, “I’ll be there for you”? Timon did. He wondered, and then he stopped wondering, and then he just stopped.

Now, I’m not saying Athens changed without him. Probably didn’t. A city like that, it rolls on. But maybe, somewhere, someone remembered the way he used to laugh, or the way he used to call everyone “friend”—even folks he barely knew. Maybe. Or maybe not. Doesn’t change much, I guess. Just—if you happen to have a friend who gives first, maybe check in once in a while. You know, before the asking gets hard and there’s nothing left but, well, regret.

You know, I’ve always thought people talk too much about things they know nothing about—like, really, if you look at last night at Netherfield, who saw anything? No one. Everyone just guesses, and, well, they act like it’s knowledge. But, the thing is, I was there, just sitting by the fireplace pretending to ignore everyone else, when Lizzy came in—you know, with her muddied skirt and all that—and, I swear, there was a hush, just for a second. Not dramatic, just—like everyone noticed something but didn’t want to admit it out loud.

Mrs. Bennet, of course, can’t keep quiet when she feels she has an audience. “My dear Jane,” she cried—really too loud for a drawing room—“if Mr. Bingley doesn’t see how devoted you are, then, truly, nothing in the world makes sense.” And Jane just kind of smiled, polite as ever, but I saw her look down at her hands. Maybe she was nervous, or maybe she just wanted everyone to stop talking for once.

Oh, and Bingley was… well, he’s always nice. I mean, almost confusingly nice, if that makes any sense. Is it possible for someone to be too agreeable? Sometimes I wonder if he has any opinions at all. Like, he just laughed at whatever anyone said, fiddled with his cuffs, and asked after the weather—again. Poor Jane tried to answer every question like it was the first time, though Lizzy shot her a look that said, “Don’t encourage him.” Not that Bingley minded. I think he’d be happy if every conversation was sort of about nothing, just floating along.

And then you’ve got Darcy—well, he stood in the corner. Really, he only talked a bit, mostly to Lizzy, and even then, it was like every word cost him a penny. You could kind of see Lizzy’s eyebrow going up as she listened, but she never lost her cool. She never does. Actually, I’m convinced she’d argue with a thunderstorm, if she thought it was being unreasonable.

Honestly, sometimes I think the people in that room must be living in a different world than I am. I mean, do they really believe what they’re saying? All that stuff about happiness and good fortune and—what was it Bingley said? “Cheerful company is the greatest delight.” As if that explains anything, or means anything at all. Maybe I’m just being grumpy. Maybe I should’ve had more lemonade.

But it gets better—or worse, depending on how you look at it. Mrs. Bennet started talking about the entail (again), and I thought, “If she says something about cousins, I’ll run into the rain.” And Jane just sat there, patient, like she was bracing herself for a storm, but Mary piped up about ‘moral worth’ (whatever that is), and the whole thing drifted away. Are people really listening to each other, or just waiting for their turn?

Oh, and did I mention how Kitty sneezed—like, three times in a row? No one said “bless you.” Everyone just stared, and then it went on as if nothing happened. I guess that’s how it always is. Stuff happens, and we all pretend it didn’t.

But, you know, after the tea and the little speeches and poor Jane trying not to look tired, Lizzy caught my eye and grinned, just for a split second. Like, a real grin—not one of those “I’m fine, everything’s fine” smiles, but more like, “Isn’t this whole thing ridiculous?” And suddenly, I didn’t mind being there so much. Sometimes having someone who gets the joke makes everything else bearable.

So yeah, maybe nothing really happened last night, and everybody’s just talking because it’s easier than saying, “I don’t know.” Or maybe that’s how things move forward—one awkward conversation at a time. Who knows? I’m just glad Lizzy was there.

Korda’s team celebrated their first title after a strong match. The tournament brought together players from many teams. It was a difficult competition. Korda finished the last round at par. This was enough to win. The team was happy after the final scores were announced. Some players said that the pressure was strong in the last holes. They needed to keep calm and focus on each shot. Korda explained that the team worked hard and supported each other. They practiced many hours before the tournament.

The changes in Afghanistan have caused many people to lose their ordinary life. The Taliban’s takeover happened quickly. There were promises at first that life would not become difficult for women. But the reality is different from what was said. Many women feel trapped. Nilofar is one of those women. She used to work as a teacher in Kabul. She talks about her problems. She says her friends have mostly left the country. Some tried to escape with their families. Nilofar did not go. She says she could not leave her old mother behind.

The Taliban imposed new rules. Women cannot work in most places. They cannot study as they did before. Those who speak out face trouble. There are stories of women arrested. People whisper about disappearances. The streets are quieter than before. Shops that sold women’s clothing are closed. Universities look empty. The faces of women are hardly seen. Many stay indoors. They fear to walk outside.

Nilofar remembers the past days. She says she used to wear bright clothes. She went to cafes with friends. Those days are gone. She tells a reporter she misses freedom. There is sadness in her words. She says, “I could not imagine this day would come.” Her friends in other countries send messages. They share photos of new lives. Nilofar feels left behind. She says, “I am alone now.”

Other women say similar things. Some had good jobs. They were doctors, journalists, lawyers. Now, most cannot continue their work. The Taliban said women will be allowed to work later. No one trusts this promise. Many women lost hope. Some families try to move daughters out of Afghanistan. It is hard to get visas. The borders are closed often. Smugglers charge high prices. Some girls leave at night. News reporters hear stories from families. Some say their daughters went missing during the journey.

Afghanistan used to have women in parliament. Now, there are none. The Taliban do not let women take part in government decisions. Some women tried to join protests. The Taliban reacted with force. Videos show women chased in the streets. Some are beaten. Some are threatened. The protests stopped because it became too dangerous.

Women who are teachers can sometimes teach girls in private homes. These lessons are risky. If the Taliban learn about them, they can come and arrest everyone. Nilofar says she tried to help some girls learn English. She decided to stop. She feared what could happen to her and the girls.

Many young women lost their dreams. Before, they planned to study abroad. They hoped to become engineers or doctors. Now, they have little hope. Some families force daughters into marriage. They say it is safer this way. Nilofar says she sees more child marriages in her neighborhood. This makes her worried. She says, “It feels like we are moving backwards.”

Friends who left Afghanistan send stories about their new lives. Some are in Europe. Some live in the United States. They have jobs. They study. They travel. Nilofar cannot join them. She says her mother is old and in poor health. She does not want to leave her behind. She tries to stay strong. Every day she prays for change.

Most women are silent. They do not talk to reporters. Some are afraid. They fear the Taliban will find out if they speak. Some change phone numbers often. Reporters say it is difficult to reach women. Those who do talk share sad stories. They tell reporters about empty classrooms, closed clinics, empty offices. They see fewer women in the streets every week.

Women used to have groups for support. Now, these groups are gone. The Taliban do not allow women’s organizations. There are less places to gather. Women try to meet in secret. They talk about old times. Some listen to music quietly at home. Nilofar says her friends used to sing together. Now, they stop singing. She says, “We are afraid all the time.”

Little girls ask their mothers why they cannot go to school. Some mothers have no answer. They say it is the rule now. The girls become sad. They play at home instead of in parks. Parks are not safe for them. The Taliban do not allow women to visit most public places. The rules change often. Every week, there is a new announcement. Women must stay home. They must cover faces. They must not talk to strangers. The rules confuse families.

Nilofar says she feels tired. She says, “I used to have dreams. Now, every day is the same.” She spends most time indoors. She watches the news on her old phone. She sees other countries. She wonders if she will ever leave Afghanistan. Her friends encourage her to stay hopeful. But she says the hope is fading. She misses her old life. She misses her friends.

On Monday, Alexei Navalny was found in a remote colony in the Arctic Circle, Russian officials said. For several weeks before, his relatives and lawyers could not communicate with him. His supporters in Moscow had concerns about his health and safety. The officials insisted Navalny was being held according to Russian law. Still, many international observers criticized the conditions and the secrecy around his transfer.

Navalny, a well-known Russian opposition leader, was moved from a penal colony near Vladimir to this facility in Yamalo-Nenets region. Russian authorities confirmed the transfer took place mid-December. His lawyer said he learned of the new location only after repeated requests for information. CNN reported that Navalny’s supporters called the new prison “one of the most severe in Russia.”

Navalny’s team said communication with him is now almost impossible. His lawyer described how the colony is difficult to reach. The nearest town is hundreds of kilometers away. Weather conditions make travel unpredictable. Human rights activists said this makes it harder to monitor Navalny’s treatment or help him if needed.

The new colony is called IK-3. It is sometimes referred to as “Polar Wolf.” Former prisoners and human rights defenders said the facility is known for strict rules and harsh discipline. CNN obtained statements from people who had served their sentences there. They described limited access to outside information and very poor conditions. Navalny’s allies said they are afraid he will face increased pressure.

Navalny’s mother said in an interview with a Russian news outlet that she worries about her son’s health. She told reporters that he already had health problems before the transfer. She said now he will face severe cold and isolation. The authorities said Navalny receives medical attention as needed. They denied all allegations of mistreatment.

Mikhail Khodorkovsky, a former Russian oligarch who also spent years in Russian detention, made a statement about Navalny. He said on social media that prisoners are often sent to very remote areas as punishment. Khodorkovsky said it is difficult for lawyers and family to visit such prisons, which he called a way for authorities to cut off prisoners from the outside world. He called for more international pressure on Russian officials regarding Navalny’s situation.

Navalny’s lawyers tried to visit him several times in December but were turned away. They said officials gave contradictory explanations for why they could not enter the colony. Sometimes they were told Navalny was “not available,” other times they were told the prison was on lockdown due to quarantine. The lawyers said they are considering a formal complaint.

The Russian penal service responded to questions from journalists. They said Navalny is being held in conditions similar to other prisoners. They stated that any claims about violations of his rights are not true. However, activists said the secrecy and lack of access point to possible problems. One activist told CNN that when a prisoner is isolated so completely, there is a risk for abuse.

Navalny is serving a long sentence for what he calls politically motivated charges. He was arrested in 2021 after returning to Russia from Germany. In Germany, he was recovering from poisoning, which he and many Western governments blamed on the Kremlin. The Russian government denied these accusations.

The United States, the European Union, and other countries have called for Navalny’s release. They said his continued detention is a sign of growing repression in Russia. Russian officials replied these statements are foreign interference. They said Navalny’s case is only about following the law.

Navalny’s supporters in Moscow organized small protests. Police quickly broke up the gatherings. Many of Navalny’s top aides have already left Russia, fearing arrest. The political climate for opposition is tense. Ordinary people said they are afraid to talk openly about Navalny.

Khodorkovsky and other former prisoners said the authorities use the penal system to silence political opponents. The transfer to remote colonies is an old method. Even so, Navalny’s team said they will continue their efforts to keep his case in public view.

Navalny’s lawyer said he hopes to visit the colony again soon. He told reporters that for now, only official information is available. The isolation of the colony makes independent confirmation impossible. International organizations called for immediate access to Navalny.

For now, concern about Navalny’s fate continues. His supporters said they would not stop speaking about his imprisonment. Russian officials have made no sign they plan to move him from the Arctic colony. The world watches for more news from the remote north.

Many people follow sports. It is common to see athletes in competitions. The Olympics are the biggest event in the world for sports. Athletes come from many countries. They want to win medals. But there are also problems. Some problems are about how people are treated. There are different groups of people. There are also people from LGBTQ communities. Recently, many talked about how sports does not always support them well. Some athletes shared their stories. They said that it was not always easy for them.

Some athletes come from LGBTQ backgrounds. Many times, they said they felt alone. Sometimes their teammates did not accept them. They worried about being open. They said there was fear. They said the sports community did not support them enough. They wanted change. One athlete, Denison, said he needed to hide his identity. He said he felt pressure. He said some women athletes have similar problems. Some do not feel safe to speak about their lives.

Sports officials responded to these issues. Some said they will try to make things better. They said they do not want discrimination. Still, many athletes feel that not enough is being done. Some athletes said that rules are not clear. They think the rules are not fair for LGBTQ athletes. They said the rules are not applied the same way for all. Denison said that sometimes officials ignore complaints. He said he tried to talk about the problems. He said people did not listen to him.

At the Olympics, there are many athletes. Some of them are LGBTQ. Some of them are women. They face pressures. Sometimes they worry about being excluded. Some athletes said that media does not always report their stories. They said media talks more about other athletes. Some feel left out. Denison said he tried to get attention for his problems. He said the media was not interested. Some women athletes also said they are not taken seriously. Some said that people doubt their abilities.

Sports organizations started to make plans. They said they want to support LGBTQ athletes. They said it is important to protect athletes from discrimination. They said they will give training. Some athletes said they want more than training. They want the rules to be changed. They want the policies to be clear. They want people to respect differences. Some athletes do not believe the changes will help. They said that plans are just words.

Some athletes said that coaches cause problems. Coaches sometimes say mean things. They do not always support athletes. Some athletes said they had bad experiences. They said they tried to complain. Complaints were not always heard. Denison said that he was told not to complain. He said he felt isolated. He said other women athletes felt the same. Some athletes left their teams because of the problems. They said they could not continue.

There are also problems with fans. Some sports fans do not accept LGBTQ athletes. Some fans make rude comments. Some fans write mean messages online. Athletes said they feel scared. They do not feel safe. They said they try to ignore the comments. But it is difficult for them. Some athletes said they wanted fans to stop. Sports officials said they will try to stop bad behavior. They said they will give warnings. Still, athletes said the problems continue.

Many athletes want more support. They want sports organizations to do more. They want people to listen to their stories. They want rules to protect them. They want media to report their problems. They said they will keep fighting. Denison said he will not give up. He said he will keep talking about his experience. He said it is important for other athletes. He said that changes will help everyone.

Some athletes also talked about their families. Some families do not support them. They said their parents did not accept their choices. They said they feel sad. They said they do not know what to do. Some athletes said they wanted to keep their lives private. They said it is difficult to live like this. Sports organizations said they will give counseling. They said they will give advice. Denison said that counseling is only a small help. He said rules need to change first.

Women athletes talked about the problems for women. They said that women are not always given fair treatment. Some said they are paid less. Some said they are given fewer chances. Some women athletes said coaches ignore their problems. They said that men are given more attention. They said they do not feel respected. Sports officials said they will give equal chances. But women athletes said they do not see much change. They said they keep asking for fairness.

Some athletes talked about injuries. They said that doctors do not take them seriously. Some said that their injuries are not treated well. Denison said he had an injury. He said doctors did not listen to him. Some women athletes said they were not believed. They said this affected their careers. They said they lost competitions because of this. They said more training is needed for doctors.

The number of rats seems to be increasing in London, according to several pest control experts. They say more reports have come in about rats being noticed during the day as well as night. Residents and business owners are speaking more often about rats showing up near homes, shops, and restaurants. Some people have sent pictures to local councils. In these photos, rats can be seen near bins, in parks, and sometimes inside buildings. Experts believe that construction projects in London have disturbed rat nests underground. When nests are disturbed, rats look for new places. They move to areas with food and shelter.

Food waste is a main reason for the rat problem. According to technicians who deal with pests, rats are attracted to bags and containers outside buildings. Restaurants and cafes sometimes leave bags out overnight. Rats tear these bags open and eat what they find inside. Experts say that smaller businesses do not always use proper bins. Some bins are broken or missing lids. When bins are not closed well, rats can get in easily. Many people in the pest control industry think that the city needs to clean more often. If trash is left out, rats will come.

The rainy weather in London also causes trouble. When there is heavy rain, rats come out from their hiding places because their nests become too wet. Pest specialists say that after rain, their phones ring more often. People complain about rats running near houses, schools, and shops. Rat numbers can become worse during wet periods. A worker from a pest control company said, “When it rains, rats are forced to move. They look for dry places. They are not picky. They will go anywhere, even homes.” Several companies agreed that calls increase after storms.

Some neighborhoods suffer more than others. Areas with older buildings are at higher risk. Old buildings have cracks and holes in the walls. Rats can squeeze through small gaps. Once inside, they search for scraps or crumbs. Houses with pets sometimes leave pet food out. Rats will eat dog food or cat food if they find it. Families tell local news they worry about disease. Rats carry germs that can cause sickness. One woman from East London said, “We see them in our backyard. My children are scared. We do not want rats in our house.” Another man said, “I have seen them outside the shop almost every day. It is bad for business.”

London councils have tried to solve the rat issue for some time. Many councils hire pest control services. These services place traps and poison around problem spots. Some people say poison is dangerous for pets and birds. Animal activists do not like the use of poison. They suggest safer methods, but these are slower and cost more. Council members explain that the rat problem may not be solved soon. As long as there is food left outside, rats will come back. Local officials advise citizens to put rubbish in bins and not leave food out. They ask business owners to keep bins closed.

There are also stories about rats getting inside the Tube. Passengers sometimes see rats running across platforms or tracks. Transport staff try to keep stations clean. Still, rats find ways inside. Engineers say that rats can live in tunnels and passageways. The underground is warm and offers many hidden spots. Sometimes, rats chew electrical wires. This causes disruptions. Transport for London admitted that rats are sometimes seen in stations. They said, “We clean every day. We do what we can, but rats are smart. They find new places to hide.” Commuters are told to report any sightings.

Pest control technicians are busy. One company said that calls about rats have doubled in the last year. They now send workers to homes, offices, and shops almost every day. They check where rats are coming in. They put traps and block holes. Some workers use cameras to find nests. Sometimes they discover several nests in one street. Workers wear masks and gloves for safety. They explain that rats are not always afraid of people. Rats become braver when they are hungry. A technician said, “Rats used to hide. Now they are seen during the day. They just walk by people.”

The government has given some money to councils to help control rats. This money pays for more traps and extra cleaning. Some councils have set up education programs.
